newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile, Mercosur erase tariffs as pact takes effect.
newsitem.headline: Chile, Mercosur erase tariffs as pact takes effect.

text.p: Trade barriers between Chile and four of its South American neighbors dropped to zero on scores of goods Tuesday as a free trade pact between the Mercosur group and Chile officially went into effect.
The agreement, signed by the presidents of the five countries in June, erased tariffs on 19 percent of all products entering Chile from Mercosur members Argentina, Brazil, Uruguay and Paraguay.
At the same time, it swept away tariffs on 15 percent of Chile's exports into Mercosur.
Other tariffs will be phased out over the next eight years, with tariffs on a few politically sensitive items like wheat and rice staying in effect for up to a further 10 years.

The implementation of the pact capped a long process in which Chile first spurned Mercosur, saying it preferred to keep its trade policies independent but then agreed to sign a free trade pact as the group gathered steam.
At Santiago's request, the agreement still falls short of making Chile a full member of Mercosur, which joins 200 million people in Latin America's biggest trading bloc.

President Eduardo Frei, who reversed his predecessors' standoffish line on Mercosur, also had to overcome strong opposition to Mercosur from Chilean farmers, who charged it would flood them with cheap Argentine and Brazilian grain.
The farmers blocked roads and burned Frei and Economy Minister Alvaro Garcia in effigy in June while the president was in Argentina to sign the accord.

Opposition in Chile has cooled since then. But the country's main farm group, the National Agriculture Society (SNA), gave a taste this week of the sort of conflict likely to become more common as Chile moves closer to Mercosur.
The SNA filed suit in court to stop imports of Argentine meat, charging sanitary code violations.

Frei has stressed the pact's benefits to Chilean consumers, who will see cheaper food prices. In a snub to Mercosur's opponents, he last week named chief Mercosur negotiator Carlos Mladinic as Chile's new agriculture minister. "Economic opening in general allows us to gain access to goods more cheaply. That's definitely the case with Mercosur," said Garcia.
Tariff reduction also has the downside of lower tax revenues.

Economist Hugo Fazio estimated the tariff cut will cost Chile about $120 million. The government will have to abandon any plans to lower its 18 percent value-added tax to maintain a fiscal surplus, he said.

The SNA says the pact will cost farmers about $460 million, even though traditional agriculture is the sector least affected by it. Chile currently has a uniform tariff of 11 percent, plus price bands for a long list of farm products, aimed at sheltering the farm sector from price fluctuations.
But economists say market forces are already leading Chile's farmers to turn their grain fields over to more export-geared crops, like fruit and vegetables.
